new_statements.quote: [p.13] Like English, Yugambeh is 'stress-timed', as are the other dialects of this language. The prominent syllables and words take more time, and the unstressed words and syllables are often slurred over. [p.14] You should note that the first syllable of a word is usually stressed and clear, except when there is a long vowel elsewhere in the word, which then gets the primary stress, and the first syllable is less clear. [p.16] Long vowels (all the ones with h written after them) are stressed; otherwise the first syllable of a word is stressed. There are never (or almost never) two long vowels in a row.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is on the first syllable; if the word contains a long vowel in a non-initial syllable, primary stress falls on that long-vowel syllable instead (and the initial syllable is reduced). At most one long vowel per word, so the rule is deterministic given vowel length. Stated for Yugambeh and explicitly extended to 'the other dialects of this language', the dictionary's coverage including Minyangbal of the Byron Bay and Brunswick River basins (= Arakwal country).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing explicit in Sharpe's own statement (the initial syllable is 'less clear' when a later long vowel takes primary stress). The reproduced older guides (Allen & Lane 1913 for Wangerriburra, p.17-18; Watson 1943, p.21) mention a secondary accent on the final/third syllable, but those are for the Beaudesert dialect, not Byron Bay.
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressed short vowels lose their 'colour' (schwa-like); tendency for u to drop from an initial unstressed syllable (kuwaŋ > kwoŋ 'rain', bulagan > blahgan); 'never (or almost never) two long vowels in a row'. Sharpe 1997:372 adds that stress perceived on a non-initial syllable in old sources 'indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed' by Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and her analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a pronunciation guide to dictionary headwords (citation forms); the language is described as stress-timed at utterance level. The statement is chain-wide (Yugambeh 'and the other dialects of this language'), not elicited specifically from Byron Bay speakers, for whom no modern phonetic record exists (the variety is extinct; Livingstone 1892 is the only dedicated grammar and is silent on accent).
new_statements.identity_note: arak1254 'Arakwal' is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping entry (ISO rkw, created 2013 on AUSTLANG/Tindale grounds): 'linguistically one of many Bandjalang varieties'. Arakwal is the name of the Byron Bay people (Arakwal Country = Broken Head to Brunswick River, per the Arakwal corporation). The speech of that area is Livingstone's 1892 'Minyung' ('spoken at Byron Bay and on the Brunswick River'), which AIATSIS The quoted stress statement (Sharpe 1998) is chain-wide for Yugambeh 'and the other dialects of this language', with the dictionary's coverage explicitly including Minyangbal of the Byron Bay and Brunswick basins; there is no Arakwal-specific phonological description, and the only dedicated grammar of the Byron Bay variety (Livingstone 1892) says nothing about accent. If catalogued, this should be entered as the Byron Bay/Minyangbal variety inheriting the Yugambeh-Bundjalung rule (and may duplicate any existing twee1234 / band1339 entry).

sources.note: The only older primary grammar of the Byron Bay ('Minyung') variety (AIATSIS files it under Arakwal E13). Opens 'The Minyug dialect is spoken at Byron Bay and on the Brunswick River'; grammar is entirely morphological (suffixes, pronouns, verbs) plus vocabulary; the only phonotactic remark is 'Every word in Minyug ends either with a vowel or a liquid'. No statement on accent or stress anywhere in the appendix (text layer searched for accent/stress/emphasis/syllable).
